name: Esther Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you truly think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Esther, 58, and I buy fresh fruit, vegetables and dairy for a wholesaler that supplies restaurants and corner shops. My day starts at 5:30 because the market doesn't wait. I call the growers and importers, I check what's ripe and what's late, and I decide how many pallets of tomatoes we'll take that morning. By ten the deals are done and then it's chasing deliveries and sorting out complaints.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the feel of it, the smell of a good load of peaches and the little victories when I get a good price. What wears me out is waste. If I order too much, it rots, and that's money in the bin. And the early starts are harder than they used to be at 58.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but overrated. We've started using a forecast tool that predicts what restaurants will order, and it's helpful about as often as the weather app. I'd tell my family it's just another tool and the market still runs on people ringing each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little uneasy. The job's okay, but restaurants are closing, margins are thin, and my boss, Gianni, is nearly 70 and will sell up one day. A new owner might streamline the buying. That has nothing to do with AI, but it keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, use the forecast to double-check my orders, and keep saving 350 a month. I'd also ask Gianni for a straight word about his plans, because it matters to us. I'd keep my mornings at the market, since that's where the good deals come from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay, nothing to panic about. I'd feel slightly worried about the future of the firm, but not about the AI. And my husband Ramón's wage as a bus driver keeps us steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a new owner could streamline the buying. What have you seen that makes you think so?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When our cousin company in the north got bought, they put two buying teams into one and let go of four people. It was all spreadsheets and savings. Gianni says he won't sell, but he's 69 and his son wants no part of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask Gianni, and how?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take him a coffee on a quiet Tuesday and ask, if you sell, would the buyers be protected? He's a straight man and he'd tell me. I'd rather know now than read it in a letter.

say: I'd say the forecast is **useful but overrated**, about as reliable as the weather app.
I'd tell family the market still runs on **people ringing each other**.
think: The real worry is **restaurants closing** and my boss Gianni, 69, selling the firm.
A new owner might **streamline** the buying, which has nothing to do with AI.
do: Use the forecast to **double-check** my orders.
Ask Gianni plainly about his **plans** over a coffee.
feel: **Okay**, with a small worry about the firm's future, steadied by Ramón's wage.
S0.quote: I'd rather know now than read it in a letter.
fieldNote: Her unease is about **ownership**, not AI: her boss is 69 and his son doesn't want the firm.
Steady with tools: uses the forecast as a **second opinion**.
A bus-driver husband gives the household a **steady** second income.

steps.text: Use the forecast tool to double-check each morning's orders
Keep buying at the market at 5:30 as usual
Save 350 a month and ask Gianni about his plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the desk work is going to be different, and the ones who learn early will be fine. I'd tell my team that planning and ordering are what the software takes first. I'd say the market and the growers aren't going anywhere, so there'll still be a place for people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think half my job is things like planning how much to order, checking invoices and answering customers, and the system will do those. What's left is the early-morning calls, the growers and fixing problems. I'd be one of the buyers who stays, if there are fewer of us. But I'm 58 and my hours are already heavy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the tool training and use it every day for a year, and I'd keep the grower relationships tight, visiting two farms in person each season. I'd ask for a shift to supplier relations, with fewer 5:30 starts. And I'd add 150 a month to savings. I'd talk to Ramón about whether he'd take more shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long hill. I'd be anxious, but I'd handle it. I'd feel a bit tired, but also determined.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd visit two farms in person each season. Why does that matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the grower who knows my face gives me the first pick when there's a short crop. A tool doesn't get you that. When the frost hit the apricots two years ago, my growers rang me before anyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa and Tim on the invoice desk, they're about 40, with kids. If the invoices are automatic, it's them first. And Zoltan, the young buyer, who's quick, but has no growers behind him yet.

say: I'd say **planning and ordering** are what the software takes first, so learn early.
I'd say the market and growers aren't going anywhere, so there's **room for people**.
think: Half my job is **planning, invoices** and answering customers, and the system will do those.
I'm 58 and the **early hours** are already heavy.
do: Take the **tool training** and use it every day for a year.
Visit **two farms** in person each season.
Add **150 a month** to savings and ask for fewer 5:30 starts.
feel: **Anxious** but able to handle it, tired and determined.
S1.quote: The grower who knows my face gives me the first pick when there's a short crop.
fieldNote: She separates her **desk tasks** from her **grower relationships** and plans to protect the second.
Her concern for **Rosa and Tim** on the invoice desk is concrete, with kids and mortgages.
Wants a shift to supplier relations, which cuts her hardest hours.

steps.text: Use the ordering tool every day after the company training
Visit two growers' farms in person each season

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is crazy and that somebody in government has to step up. I'd say in the group chat that we should look after each other. I wouldn't say too much at work, I'd keep my head down and see what the firm does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the buying desk goes in two years, mine included. Ramón's job would hold for a while, robots take three more years for driving, but we can't live on a bus driver's wage alone. We have a mortgage and my daughter's university fees. Four months of savings isn't much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut costs hard, stop the holiday fund, and go to Gianni about the firm's plans. I'd ask what hands-on jobs there might be, such as quality checking at the market or running the cold store. I'd talk to my kids and tell them to keep their own work flexible. I'd also use whatever government help there is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like standing on a train platform when the train is already moving. I'd be anxious and a bit angry, but I wouldn't go to pieces. I've got three kids and a husband, and I'd keep it together for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said quality checking or the cold store. Why those?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they're hands-on, so the robots take longer to get there, and they use what I know about produce. I can tell ripe from rotten at a glance. A machine will learn that eventually, but I've got three or four more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter at university?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to stay, because her degree is her future, and we'll find the money. I'd cut my own spending before hers. But I'd also say, pick something with hands or with people, not just a screen.

say: I'd say **two years** is crazy and the government must step up.
At work I'd **keep my head down** and watch what the firm does.
think: The buying desk goes in two years, **mine included**.
We can't live on a **bus driver's wage** alone, with a mortgage and university fees.
do: Cut costs hard and stop the **holiday fund**.
Ask Gianni about **quality-checking** or cold-store jobs.
Use **government help** if there is any.
feel: **Anxious** and a bit angry, but I'd keep it together for the kids.
S2.quote: I can tell ripe from rotten at a glance. A machine will learn that eventually, but I've got three or four more years.
fieldNote: She expects the desk to go but looks for a **hands-on** role where her produce knowledge counts.
Her daughter's **university fees** are the hard cost she protects.
Steady, practical and protective, with little anger beyond the **initial** reaction.

steps.text: Stop the holiday fund and cut spending hard
Ask about quality checking or running the cold store
Apply for any government help for laid-off workers
Protect my daughter's university fees by cutting my own spending first

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair bit of time to plan, if people take it seriously. I'd tell the team to look at what they can learn. And I'd say Gianni should plan for it too, because we'd all need to know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have a role until about 2031 if I stay sharp, and I'd be 63. I could aim to retire early if the cushion's right. I'm not worried about myself, I'm worried about the younger buyers and the firm itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tool and push for a role teaching it to the others. I'd pay down the mortgage faster and keep the grower trips as my special part. And I'd ask Ramón to plan his retirement with me for around 2031. I'd also take on the cold-store training as a back-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels manageable, a bit like planning for winter. I'm uneasy, but I have a plan. I'd feel okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push for a role teaching the tool. Why would the firm agree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twelve buyers would need training, and using me is cheaper than paying an outside trainer. I'm already the one they ask. And I'd stay on the payroll during the change, which helps me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you pay down first, and by how much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage, about 400 a month extra. We have eleven years left on it, so it'd bring that down to about eight. Ramón is 61 and he'd like to stop at 65, so we want to be debt-free by then.

say: I'd say **five years** is time to plan, if people take it seriously.
I'd say Gianni should plan too, because we all need to **know**.
think: I'd have a role until about **2031** if I stay sharp.
I worry more about the **younger buyers** than about myself.
do: Push for a role **teaching the tool** to colleagues.
Pay **400 a month** extra on the mortgage.
Take the **cold-store training** as a back-up.
feel: **Uneasy** but with a plan, like preparing for winter.
S3.quote: Twelve buyers would need training, and using me is cheaper than paying an outside trainer.
fieldNote: Five years lets her plan with **Ramón** around a debt-free retirement.
Positions herself as an **internal trainer**, using her steady tool skills as a lever.
The firm's **size** and Gianni's age remain her main uncertainty.

steps.text: Offer to train the other buyers on the ordering tool
Pay 400 a month extra on the mortgage
Take the cold-store supervisor training as a back-up
Plan retirement with Ramón for around 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time and I wouldn't lose sleep. I'd tell my kids to plan their careers around people and hands, not just a screen. I'd tell my friends we should keep an eye on it, but not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fine. I'd be 68 by then, long retired. My concern is Gianni's firm, because it may not last that long as a family business, and my pension depends on the firm's pension scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job, use the tools as they come and put money in the company pension. I'd retire at 63 or 64, then maybe do a few market mornings for fun. I'd ask the firm about the pension protection if the firm is sold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels calm, with a little knot about the pension. I'd feel lucky to be on this side of the timeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your pension depends on the firm. What worries you about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm is sold, the new owner could change the scheme. I've paid in for twenty-six years. I'd want a letter saying what happens, and I'd bring Ramón to the meeting as a second pair of ears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about careers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something that needs hands and trust, like nursing or electrics or running a small shop. Be curious about the tools too. And keep some savings, always some, because nothing's guaranteed.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty of time and I wouldn't lose sleep.
I'd tell my kids to plan careers around **people and hands**.
think: I'd be 68 by then and **long retired**.
My concern is the firm's **pension scheme** if it's sold.
do: Keep doing the job and add to the **company pension**.
Retire at **63 or 64** and maybe do some market mornings.
Ask for **pension protection** if the firm is sold.
feel: **Calm**, with a small knot about the pension, and lucky to be on this side.
S4.quote: Learn something that needs hands and trust, like nursing or electrics or running a small shop.
fieldNote: The decade reaches past her retirement, so **her job** is safe; her **pension** is the open worry.
Her advice to her kids is the clearest, and she repeats it in every **long** scenario.
Wants documents, not reassurance, and will bring Ramón as a witness.

steps.text: Keep buying and use the tools as they arrive
Add to the company pension each month
Retire at 63 or 64 and do occasional market mornings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because there'd be no chance to get ready. What would help is a clear plan from the firm, retraining that someone else pays for, and a safe pension. And some help for the kids who are just starting out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. Only that I'm a practical person and I try to take things as they come. But I'd like people in charge to be straight with us.

headlineQuote: I'm a practical person and I try to take things as they come. But I'd like people in charge to be straight with us.
portrait: Esther, 58, buys **fresh produce and dairy** for a wholesaler serving restaurants and corner shops, starting at 5:30 each morning.
Centre in outlook and steady with new tools, she uses a forecast tool **as a second opinion**.
She has about four months saved, a bus-driver husband, Ramón, and a daughter at **university**.
Her main worry in the mild worlds is the **firm's future**, since her boss is nearly 70.
Her mood rises to **anxious** when AGI is two years away and eases when the timeline reaches retirement.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because there'd be no time to get ready with a daughter in university.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **plan** from the firm, paid retraining, and a **safe pension**.
